title: Affine realizability geometry uses raw W_enc, so the behaviorally null all-ones (mean) direction dominates c_free, kappa, c_qp, c_dec and enc_dec_cos in the primary GPT-2 setting
evidence: In the jb GPT-2 L6 SAE, every one of the 24576 W_enc columns has a positive component along 1/sqrt(d). The median |cos| with that direction is 0.73 (p99 0.82). The data never constrains this direction: training and analysis inputs are exactly mean-centred (HFModel.resid centres; TL center_writing_weights), so the component acts only as an extra bias. Every later read of the GPT-2 residual goes through a LayerNorm that subtracts the mean, so adding c*1 to the stream is exactly null for behavior (the HFModel docstring says so too). analyze_position_affine still uses J = W_enc^T at line 72/83 and gain = W_T.dhat at line 152, which lets edits exploit this null direction. I restricted edits to mean-zero deltas (W -> C W_enc, C = I - 11^T/d) on 16 cached-residual cases: kappa fell from 1.43 to 1.03, 1.59 to 1.02, 1.41 to 1.02, 1.20 to 1.01 and 1.38 to 1.02; c_free rose 30-90% (5.31 to 10.06); c_qp went from 5.33 to 6.67; c_dec went from 58.0 to 41.7 and from 36.1 to 26.9. With A non-empty, the artifact kappa is about 1/sqrt(1 - 0.73^2), roughly 1.46: c_free can use the 1-direction, but c_lin cannot, because every protected feature shares it. Caveat: the cases were per-text mean residuals from results/cache featstats, not per-position residuals, because GPT-2 was not run.
failure_scenario: 05_realizability.py on gpt2_relu_jb_L6 (real positions, L0 about 50). The pre-registered H2 diagnostics are then contaminated: median kappa, exact-QP cost, decoder collateral and the encoder-decoder-cosine baseline. The reported T/P 'interference' (kappa about 1.4-1.6) is mostly a property of the SAE's bias-like 1-direction, not of feature geometry the model can see. With the null direction removed, kappa is about 1.02, so H2 correlations and any 'interference exists' conclusion would be driven by an artifact, which is likely correlated with feature density, one of the H2 baselines. The same root cause likely affects enc/pinv/ridge/opt in methods.py: for K=1, pinv = enc puts about 53% of its norm-matched energy into the null direction. Their encoder self-consistency scores, measured on h + delta with its mean component, would also be spuriously good, which is exactly the 'encoder score improves but behavior does not' pattern the user wants to detect.
fix: For settings whose model is invariant to the residual mean (GPT-2 with centring; not Gemma/RMSNorm, and the LN TopK Jacobian already contains C), analyze the SAE on the canonical edited state C(h + delta). Use W = C @ W_enc in analyze_position_affine (or add the equality 1^T delta = 0 to Jeq), compute the dec gain with C @ dhat, and run the qp_check / dec collateral through sae.encode(center(h + x)) instead of pre + W^T x. Add a 'mean_invariant' flag to the setting and apply the same projection in methods.py Jacobians (pre_jacobian for norm='none') and in the internal metrics in evaluate.py. Re-run the realizability summary and the H2 diagnostics afterwards.

title: TopK+LN decoder cost comes from a coarse upward-only 1.25x line search: c_dec is overestimated (median 1.22x) and dec collateral is measured at the overshoot
evidence: Under LN, adding c*dhat inflates std, so the first-order c from rT/gain nearly always undershoots and the loop takes at least one multiplicative 1.25 step. On 96 TopK cases (cached per-text mean residuals, 16 concepts x K in {1,3} x 3), I bisected along dhat for the exact smallest c that reaches the target. c_dec divided by that minimum had median 1.22, mean 1.18 and max 1.25; 84% of cases were above 1.05. Because collateral is measured at the inflated c, dec_P_lost was inflated as well (reported vs exact-c: 10 vs 7, 19 vs 14, 12 vs 8, 10 vs 8). Other problems in the same block: success is tested on pre (p3[T] >= tau) rather than on activation (T must actually be in the top-k after the edit). If the loop never succeeds, dec_P_rel_change, dec_P_lost and dec_new_active are still written, evaluated at about 1.25^29 times the first-order scale, even though c_dec = inf; the affine path omits these fields in that case. A first-order gain <= 0 is also taken as unreachable, which is a local Taylor conclusion reported as a finite-step one.
failure_scenario: In the TopK robustness setting, the decoder-steering cost and collateral are systematically about 20% worse than the true values along the same direction. Meanwhile the GN solution is exact, so every 'dec vs constrained' cost/collateral comparison and the TopK H2 'decoder collateral' diagnostic are biased against dec. Any aggregate of dec collateral also mixes in the values from the huge failed scales.
fix: Bracket first (grow c until the true forward reaches the target at the activation level, i.e. f3[T] >= tau - tol with T in the top-k), then bisect to a relative tolerance of about 1e-4. Record collateral at the bisected c. When the target is not reachable within the bracket, set the collateral fields to NaN. Do not use the first-order gain sign as a reachability test under LN: always try the true forward along dhat.

title: Solver non-optimal statuses (user_limit, infeasible_inaccurate) and solver failures are reported as geometric infeasibility, and optimal_inaccurate is accepted as exact
evidence: In cvxpy 1.9.3, Clarabel MAX_ITERATIONS/MAX_TIME map to 'user_limit' with no exception, so there is no OSQP fallback. exact_qp returns None for every status except optimal/optimal_inaccurate, and analyze_position_affine (lines 127-136) then sets qp_feasible=False and c_qp=inf. Only an exception triggers the OSQP fallback, and an exception raised inside that fallback is not caught, which aborts the whole 05 run with no per-position guard. Constraint generation drops working-set constraints from the violation check (setdiff1d with work, line 117), so an inaccurate solve that violates a working constraint can still be declared converged.
failure_scenario: A badly scaled position, for example Gemma with pre about 850 and thresholds about 245, makes Clarabel stop at max_iter or return infeasible_inaccurate. The position is counted as 'not realizable' (c_qp=inf), which inflates the reported infeasibility fraction and the median exact-QP cost used in H2. Or a SolverError inside the OSQP fallback crashes the realizability script partway through a setting.
fix: Map only status == 'infeasible' to qp_feasible=False. For user_limit, *_inaccurate and solver errors, set qp_feasible=None (undetermined) and keep the status. Wrap the fallback in try/except. After the final round, check every accepted x against all (T, A, I) constraints with an explicit tolerance before setting qp_feasible=True. Consider scaling the problem (divide by |h|) for Gemma.

title: qp_within_budget is computed from a relaxation lower bound when constraint generation did not converge, and the last round's solution is never checked
evidence: If the loop ends at max_rounds, c_qp = ||x|| of the last relaxed QP, which is only a lower bound, and qp_feasible=None. qp_over_lin (line 148) and qp_within_budget (line 166) still use this lower bound, so qp_within_budget can be True for an undetermined case. The loop also solves on round max_rounds and exits without checking that solution for violations, so a feasible final solution is reported as not converged.
failure_scenario: Large edits at positions where more than 60x48 inactive constraints are needed. These are rare given the observed 2-3-round convergence, but most likely at large Delta or K=3. They get counted as 'realizable within budget' while unresolved, which biases the within-budget fraction upward.
fix: Run one more violation check after the loop. Set qp_within_budget (and qp_over_lin) to None when qp_feasible is None, or report them only for converged cases.

title: The jb ReLU SAE's Jacobian is dominated by the all-ones direction, which GPT-2 ignores, so the constrained methods only look constrained
evidence:
Measured on jb gpt2-small-res-jb L6 (weights from hf_cache). For every one of the 24576 W_enc columns, the component along 1/sqrt(d) is positive, with a median of 73% of the column norm. The top singular value of W_enc is 318; the next is 28.8. The SAE was trained on centred residuals (TransformerLens center_writing_weights; the HF hook also centres h), so this direction was never constrained.

In GPT-2 the direction has no effect, because every read of the residual stream goes through a LayerNorm. I checked this with HFModel(layer=5, center=True): adding 50*1/sqrt(d) at every position changed the logits by at most 6e-5. A centred random edit of norm 5 changed them by 3.9.

pre_jacobian with norm=='none' returns the raw W_enc rows (lines 148-149, via pre() at lines 88-92). As a result, pinv, ridge, *_fs, dec_proj_randP and opt (methods.py 191-227, 259-288) meet J_P delta=0 and the finite-step constraints partly by moving along 1. Results on 21 real positions, alpha = 0.45 x median norm, raw vs mean-removed delta:
- pinv: pRel 0.000 and 0 lost features, vs 0.27-0.31 and 24-28 lost per position.
- pinv_fs / dec_proj_fs: 1-3 new active features and pRel 0, vs 54-91 new and pRel 0.37-0.57. That is worse than dec, which has pRel 0.33-0.36.
- The mean component that causes this is only about 1-1.5 norm units out of 35.

The same root cause affects realizability.py:77 (W = sae.W_enc). There kappa is 1.41-1.63 raw vs 1.07-1.09 with a centred encoder, and c_free is about 30% too low.
failure_scenario: This affects the dev1 sweep now running on gpt2_relu_jb_L6 and the realizability/H2 analysis. The run would report that pinv, *_fs and opt preserve the protected features exactly and remove new activations, and that this internal success does not carry over to behaviour. That dissociation would be an artefact: along the directions the model can actually see, the corrected edits change protected features as much as dec or more. The H2 diagnostics (median kappa, QP cost) would also be inflated by a direction the model ignores. Both H1 and H2 conclusions could flip.
fix:
For SAEs trained on centred residuals (the jb setting; add a flag from pinned.json):
- Centre the input inside SAEWrap.pre (x = h - h.mean(-1)).
- Make pre_jacobian return centred rows (W - W.mean over d) for norm=='none'.
- Project every method's delta onto 1-perp before norm matching.
- Use the centred W_enc in realizability.analyze_position_affine.

Then re-run the dev sweep and the realizability analysis. Leave Gemma (RMSNorm) and the OAI LayerNorm SAE unchanged.

title: enc is not really norm-matched: 51-70% of its squared norm is along the all-ones direction
evidence:
g_T = sum_t w_t W_enc[:,t] with raw jb columns. On 21 real positions, 51-70% of ||delta||^2 lies along 1/sqrt(d), with a mean component of +25 to +27 at alpha = 0.45 x median norm (35.5). The effective (centred) norm is therefore only 0.55-0.70 x alpha. The internal numbers are inflated as well:
- tgt_gain 49.4 raw vs 21.6 with the mean removed (topic:5, K=1).
- new_active 24528 per position (every feature) vs 356-867.
- pRel 9.1-9.8 vs 0.55-0.73.
The pilot log shows the same thing (enc new=24514).
failure_scenario: When enc is compared with dec, diffmean and the others at the same alpha grid (up to 0.9), it is actually running at roughly 0.6x strength. Its behavioural dose-response and its alpha chosen on dev are therefore biased. Its internal scores are the largest of any method only because of the ignored direction, which feeds a false 'internal gain without behaviour' pattern for the encoder-gradient baseline.
fix: Use centred encoder rows (this follows from the saes.py fix), or at least set delta <- delta - delta.mean(-1) and renormalise to alpha, whenever the SAE and model live in centred coordinates.

title: Internal metrics are computed on h+delta without removing the mean, so a tiny ignored component dominates them
evidence:
_collect encodes h + delta as is, but the model is invariant to delta's all-ones component and the jb encoder is very sensitive to it (about 2 units of pre-activation per unit of mean component, for every feature). On 21 real positions at alpha = 0.45, raw vs mean-removed delta:
- dec: 16-38 lost and 17-19 new per position, vs 7-20 lost and 69-99 new.
- random: new_active 49.5 or 2720 depending only on the sign of random_dir's mean component (-0.90 vs +3.28, which varies by concept seed). After centring it is 66-157.
- ridge: 3552-4224 new vs 97-356.
err_norm_ratio and err_delta_frac (lines 319-323) have the same problem.
failure_scenario: The 'encoder self-consistency' arm (int_tgt_gain, int_p_rel_change, int_new_active_per_pos, int_err_*) is used in the NO_GO rule ('improvements only in encoder metrics') and to contrast internal scores with behaviour. These numbers mostly reflect how much of each method's delta falls along 1 and with what sign, not collateral damage the model can see. Method rankings on internal metrics, including dec vs random vs the constrained methods, can reverse.
fix: Measure internal metrics on the canonical representation. For centred-coordinate settings, compute pre2, f2 = sae.encode_full(h + (delta - delta.mean(-1, keepdim=True))), or centre inside SAEWrap.pre as in the saes.py fix. Report the fraction of ||delta||^2 along 1 as a diagnostic.

title: opt's fixed candidate set misses almost every feature that opt actually turns on, so the new-activation penalty does nothing
evidence:
The candidates are a fixed top-512 by |d_T.W_enc| + |g_T.W_enc|/||W_enc||. Because of operator precedence, only the second term is normalised. That term is dominated by the shared all-ones component: median 0.85 vs 0.056 for the decoder term. The resulting candidates barely overlap with those from a centred encoder (77-123 of 512).

On 21 real positions (jb, alpha = 0.45), only 0.06-0.2% of the features opt newly activates are in the candidate set. Even with a centred W, only 2-6% of dec's newly activated features would be. Because the penalty relu(pre - thr) is applied only to candidates, the mu_new term has almost no effect. opt ends with 117-338 new features per position, vs 17-19 for dec (raw metric).
failure_scenario: 'opt' is meant to be the direct activation-optimisation baseline (task item 3). In practice it optimises target gain under the linear P projection and ignores collateral activation. So opt vs the linear/fs methods (and any 'direct optimisation doesn't help' conclusion) compares against a strawman, not the stated objective.
